newsitem.title: UK: Britain moves to remodel pension provision.
newsitem.headline: Britain moves to remodel pension provision.

text.p: Pension provision in Britain is set for its biggest shake-up since the second world war following the launch on Thursday of a wide-ranging pensions review by the government.
Central to the review will be the government's belief that the way ahead lies in people having access to a second pension to supplement the basic state pension.
Secretary of State for Social Security, Harriet Harman, said the government would consult widely on proposals for 'stakeholder pensions' which it pledged to set up in its election manifesto.
Government sources said the new pensions would be provided by an alliance of employer and employee organisations and financial services companies.

They would offer "secure, flexible and value-for-money" pensions and meet the needs of those unable to join an employer's occupational scheme, those on modest incomes or in changing employment patterns.
They could also provide a vehicle for smaller firms to make pensions provision for their employees.
"We recognise that, for many people, security in retirement can best be achieved by building their own funded second pension," Harman said.
The government is also proposing 'citizenship pensions' aimed at those, for example, caring for elderly relatives and unable to contribute to pensions in their own right.
Harman said both proposals would be legislated for and implemented in the current session of Parliament, expected to last until late 2001 or early 2002.
The government promised that pensioners' organisations, employers, employees, consumers pensions experts would all have a chance to participate fully in the review.
"Only by achieving a sustainable consensus for change can the country meet the pensions challenge" said Harman.
The initial framework for change will be published in the first half of 1998.
But the government said it would stand by its manifesto commitment to retain the basic state pension and the state earnings related pension scheme (Serps).
The review is an attempt to head off the problems caused by an ageing population.
The basic state pension is expected to cost 31.9 billion pounds ($53.5 billion) this year, roughly one third of the total social security budget.
A recent report by the Office of Fair Trading found that around 25 percent of the workforce had no pension provision.
Another task for the review will be to establish "the right balance between public and private sectors".
This is likely to involve deciding what the government's role will be in approving providers of the new pensions.

The requirement of value for money, security and flexibility is likely to mean companies only being allowed to sell these pensions if they meet certain criteria on financial strength, charges, investment and service performance.

The government has hinted in the past that companies failing to meet its December 1998 deadline for settling compensation claims arising from the pensions mis-selling scandal of the late 1980s and 1990s could be excluded from provision of new second pensions.
The crisis in pension provision in Britain was highlighted by a damning OFT report on the shortcomings of existing pension products published earlier this week.
It called for radical changes to safeguard consumer interests and for the government to incorporate a new, flexible pension product.
Harman said the government wanted to support and strengthen the existing framework of occupational pension provision.
This might involve establishing a benchmark against which employers, employees and trustees could measure their own scheme, she said.
